Title: A returning player's comments on the new rulings...

Messages.Author: David and Carlene Elliott
Messages.Body:
I am an old Jyhad player who has recently returned to the game, just
in time, it seems, for a major upheaval in the game environment. I
started playing Jyhad before I ever played that other card game, and
grew to think of it as the intellectual game of choice for card
floppers. What I loved about it was the variety of strategies that could
be employed, just the fact that sometimes a political deck could survive
to trounce a combat deck made my day! I didn't always win, nor did I
want to. I was there because it was fun. Every game I played was
different, and that was the true allure of Jyhad. I stopped playing it
when I became interested in being competitive. Quite frankly I never saw
Jyhad as being a serious tournament game, competitive players were
usually the first to be ousted. Magic filled the competitive void for
me, Jyhad was the game I fell back on when I got sick of playing the
same old deck types in Magic, and just wanted something more inventive
and interactive.
I have been following this newsgroup for awhile now, and reading the
posts here are what prompted me to get back into this game. This week I
went out and spent $200 on the expansion sets after reading about all
those wonderful power cards that you simply must have. Again, I wasn't
interested in being competitive, I just liked the idea of new and
powerful combinations. I was ecstatic after being able to come up with
two Tomb of Ramses and a Return to Innocence! Not to mention that I
would get to try all those other great cards I had heard about. Last
night, I played my first Jyhad game in 3 years, and I loved it! The
local group had their own house rules which were easy to follow and made
the game fun. I can't wait to go back next Thursday.
But today I got an unexpected shock. The rules team has just turned my
$200 re-investment and delight, into a pile of near worthless cards and
discontent! I realize that maybe I haven't been around recently to
observe the abusive combinations in action, but I can't believe that
things were EVER this bad! They have actually re-written the card text
on these cards to the point that it makes no sense to play them, lest I
have to carry around an extensive rules listing with which to refer to
every five minutes. How is this supposed to lure anyone into this game?
Well, a solution hit me after reading through the fifty or so
complaints against the rulings, something so simple as to be overlooked:
don't use 'em. People, we are the ones who decide whether or not we wish
to spend our money and time on this game, and we should be the ones to
keep the game fun. As I have said before, I do not wish to make this a
competitive venture, I only want it to be fun. Binders of errata and
rules changes are NOT fun. In my new group, they do not subscribe to
this or any other newsgroup, but we have a great way of keeping abusive
card combos to minimum; we restrict the number of them in a deck. It is
the simplest and most effective way of doing what the rules team is
attempting. It has always been my experience that in this game
everything has a counter, it's just a mixture of luck and deck building
skill as to whether or not you have that counter.
So, for me and mine, we will continue to play the cards as they are
written. I choose not to except their rules. The game was fun before and
it can be again, just use common sense and police your own play group.
Do as a true methuselah would and hold a vote. Remember, it is YOU who
have the power to decide whether or not to accept the changes.
Hey, you know what? Suddenly those Tomb of Ramses don't look so bad
anymore! Maybe these cards aren't worthless after all.

Dave

I think it's perfectly right to play housrules with friends. I do it
myself.
But I think different on the tournament-issue. I believe that tournaments
are very important for a CCG, especially for V:TES. And therefore it's
important for players at tourneys that they play with a common set of
rules, be they whatever they are. The point is: if everyone plays with
the same rules, then everyone has the same "disadvantage" with rulings on
certain cards. Don't you find this a solid basis to begin with?

Let's take a closer look on tournaments.
What are they good for? I think they give a sign that a game isn't dead.
A tournament is a visible thing, for players, spectators, and the company
which hopefully supports/sanctions it.
Of course, nobody wants to play tournaments every day, but once every
month or every two month, people are eager to meet on a competitive basis.

That said, in Vienna (Europe), people like to play sealed-deck tourneys.
In fact we had only one "standard" tourney so far, as players don't like
to play NL. Whereas with sealed deck they still play NL, but it is more
fun. We played Sabbat (4 or 5 booster), Sabbat draft, V:TES-sealed (2
starters) and even "expansion-mixes".

Sealed tournaments serve two purposes: firstly, players get the thrill
from the tourney without broken combos. (If a broken card shows up, it
is not likely to come in a combo!) Our people like it that way (and we
have a _large_ V:TES community). Secondly, players get new cards in a
pleasant manner, and the retailer can sell his stock (which is the
most important thing at all: if the retailer re-orders, that's a sign
to the company).

I urge every group to try sealed-deck tournaments, you'll see how much
fun that is.

Next, if you feel a bit adventurous, you can try a thing we often do:
a number of players in our group buys a fixed number of boosters and
starters (usually we buy 2 starters or 1 Starter and 3-4 boosters)
construct decks out of this limited pool of cards and start playing
against each other in what order they like (e.g. 6 players participate,
but only 4 meet on a regular basis, whereas the other two meet regular with
2 of the former 4). The important thing is: they play for ante, to get
some thrill. (Sadly, I lost Giants Blood and Pulled Fangs on one evening,
but it was fun nevertheless.) After a few weeks this "campaign" ends when
the group feels one player has too good cards or it gets boring.
Try it! This helps our beloved game!

Sam, you shouldn't detest WotC. It's not worth it, believe me. If you
want the game prosper, then go out and advertise it, as we do.

It's a pity you do not contribute to this list often (if at all).
But "lurking" and knowing what's going on is better than ignoring
the developments in the game.

that don't show up in this newsgroup.

-Carl

> > The local group had their own house rules which were easy to follow

But why did they have house rules? Most likely, because they recognized
that there are some slight card-specific problems with the game that
were not sufficiently addressed prior to these new rulings. I think
most people are upset because LSJ didn't choose "their" house rules, and
some stranger's house rules are being imposed on them. This is
perfectly understandable. Everyone wants to play the game the way they
think is best. But it's best to have one consistent, balanced way to
play the game. LSJ's rules make the game balanced. Not everyone agrees
with his methods, but I don't think that anyone strongly objects to the
rulings on the basis that the game is _still_ broken under them.

> > They have actually re-written the card text
> > on these cards to the point that it makes no sense to play them,
> > lest I have to carry around an extensive rules listing with which to
> > refer to every five minutes.

Except that after a while you will remember them, or someone else will.
Cards with extensive changes are rare; I think there were less than a
dozen. And now that they're not totally broken anymore, you won't see
them every five minutes. There will always be someone (and it may
eventually be you!) who knows all of the rulings by heart. It's the
nature of things that some people like to be rules lawyers. And I would
say that only the new Tomb, RtI, and Mind Rape wordings are hard to
remember.

> > complaints against the rulings, something so simple as to be
> > overlooked: don't use 'em. People, we are the ones who decide
> > whether or not we wish to spend our money and time on this game,
> > and we should be the ones to keep the game fun.

How are you going to keep the game fun? How are you going to prevent
abuses of Tomb, RtI, Fame, etc.? With your own house rules? Why are
yours better than LSJ's? I'm not trying to be combative here, but it
doesn't make any sense to me.

> > Binders of errata and
> > rules changes are NOT fun.

Except that LSJ's recent additions are what? Two or three pages of
text? Hardly _binders_ worth.

> > In my new group, they do not subscribe to

> > abusive card combos to minimum; we restrict the number of them in a
> > deck. It is the simplest and most effective way of doing what the

Restricting broken cards doesn't make them any less broken. You just
don't see them as often.

> > It has always been my experience that in this game
> > everything has a counter, it's just a mixture of luck and deck
> > building skill as to whether or not you have that counter.

If a card is so powerful that you have to go out of your way to build
your deck to stop that card, then that card is too powerful. How do I
deal with Return to Innocence? Put in bleed bounce? But what if I
wanted to build a deck without Dominate or Auspex? I guess I'm just out

> > So, for me and mine, we will continue to play the cards as they are
> > written. I choose not to except their rules. The game was fun before
> > and it can be again, just use common sense and police your own play
> > group.

Then for every play group in the world there is a different game being
played. Tournaments with significant numbers of people are hence
impossible, and every time someone wants to go from one group to
another, they have to change their decks and deck-building philosophy to
deal with the new rules.

This, I think, is another fundamental philosophical difference. The 'no-
broken' camp (of which you are the most [dare i say the only] articulate,
generally sensible member), has this 'slippery slope' view of a progressive
downward spiral of hosing the most powerful card *at the moment*. I,
and I suspect others, disagree. *Because* the cost/power ratios of cards
are compared, one sees that once egregious excursions like the Infamous
Four (RtI, TB, ToRIII, MR) are dealt with, the cardset is largely *in*
balance.

Case in point: No-one's been arguing for the next round of 'overpowerful'
cards so far. The recurring joke in the M*g*c newsfroups, lo these years
agone, was 'BAN THE PEARLED UNICORN!!!' It was a joke then, and more so now.
I don't think anyone's going to make noises to ban plain brown Dodge,
or even Force of Will now that Fame's been fixed.

That being said, I think giving Fortitude bleed is like giving Potence
intercept -- it's weird and it tastes funny. But the card is printed, and
I don't have a problem with its power level.

>Sure. In the same way, I build my decks to pre-empt, counter or deflect
>big bleeds, to destroy or purloin locations, and to intercept, over-vote
>or cancel political actions. Coincidentally or not, they are effective
>against RtI's. The last time I saw one in a tournament, my predator was
>discarding it.

The difference, I think, is that one's defence structure can usually be
allowed to fail once in the mid-game without catastrophic consequence, while
RtI allows catastrophic consequence to occur significantly earlier in the game
than other cards. In conjunction with cards that ameliorate or eliminate
the admittedly large cost (Mind Rape, Possession), the risk/reward
ratio is thrown out of proportion.

Different cards have different power levels; hence their different
costs. Return to Innocence, however, has a power level exceeding the
game's ability to impose a reasonable cost in vampire blood -- thus
it imposes an additional cost that is readily avoided, and winds up
being undercosted.

gomi

I agree that the argument is an impasse. This is what I see as why (and
I'm probably mostly just restating your position above):

You (and some others) don't like the new rulings, or don't like having
rulings designed to 'balance' the game, because you don't see 'balance'
as a desirable quality in Jyhad.

I, and some others, believe that 'balance' is the coolest quality Jyhad
has as a game. The cardset was (and could now be again) such that
the relative power levels of cards was very even for the most part; there
were (should be, in our opinion) no cards that are lots better than other
comparable cards; no cards that break the appropriate-cost-for-appropriate-
effect model that seemed to govern Jyhad. The result of this was a
game where any number of different focused decktypes could be very
successful, because the cards they used as building blocks, and the
strategies that could be built out of those cards, were essentially
balanced with regards to each other.

You seem to feel that it's not really important whether or not it's
possible to 'abuse' the rules, to construct 'dishonorable' decks that
win a lot by using overpowered cards, because it's only a game. To
some of us, what makes it an *enjoyable* game is the balanced quality
it has (or should have).

Because we don't really agree on what it is that makes Jyhad good in
the first place, we naturally end up disagreeing on how (and whether)
to balance the rules and the cards. And that's why we see increasingly
heated arguments on this newsgroup: because people start yelling at
each other because they don't understand why their opponents can't see
the points they're trying to make.

From our point of view, there *are* a priori considerations at work
in card design and relative costing. Because of that, it's reasonable
to make arguments about the cards based solely on logical analysis, as
well as based on empirical results.

It's because we're starting from different assumptions. It shouldn't
be surprising that they lead us to different conclusions.

But if you're interested in seeing some empirical data, that's all good
too, since we 'theory-oriented balance' types are generally interested
in facts too, at least sometimes. ;-)

Josh

> new ones don't automatically pop up. One can very easily have a whole
> forest of cards with power levels close to "3", and a few with power
> levels "4", or "5". If you weaken/ban all the 4s and 5s, the
> remaining 3s are fine -- "broken" doesn't mean most powerfull, just
> too powerfull.
>
> IMNO this is how Jyhad is now, a bunch of power "3" cards.

While I agree with you in general, I think you overstate your case. There
remains a significant amount of power variation in V:tES. Some cards will
have more effect on the game than others, and this is not necessarily a
bad thing. I might, for instance, arbitrarily create the following power
scale:

1: These cards are complete wallpaper. Even if you design a deck
specifically to make use of them, you can always improve the deck
by taking them out and putting in something else. Unlike broken
cards, they are not a problem, as they can safely be ignored.
They are merely a design mistake that affects the game only by
reducing your number of available card choices by one.

2: These cards are significantly less powerful than average, and do
not see play very often. However, they are occasionally useful
in very specialized decks.

3: Average power. Useful in some decks, not in others.

4: A popular card of above average power. Seen in more than the
average number of decks and often useful in multiples. Its
popularity has a discernible effect on the metagame, with cards
that counter it becoming increasingly popular as well, until its
power is checked. It is not, however, useful in all competitive
deck designs, and not all decks will be make more competitive by
its inclusion.

5: Broken Card. This card will make most decks more competitive with
few exeptions, and give those decks such a strong edge that
strategies that cannot use the card become significantly less
competitive by comparison. It is so discernibly better than many
"Power 3" cards, that it can improve almost deck by replacing a
power 3 card. Too many such "broken" cards reduce game variety by
turning "2"s and "3"s into wallpaper by comparison, such that
most cards printed are excluded from consideration when designing
a deck.

While perfect balance would be ideal, it is not attainable, and Legbiter
is right that there will always be a few cards that are most powerful.

But there are degrees of balance, and the more game balance you have, the
greater is game variety and player design choice. The ultimate broken
card imaginable would be one so powerful that one could put 80 of them in
your library and be guaranteed to win against anyone who did not adopt the
same strategy (essetially reducing variety to nil). Ultimate balance
would be where all of the aproximately 1000 printed cards see game play
with equal frequency.

I do not expect ultimate balance. I expect a few cards to be wallpaper,
though hopefully not many. I would like the game to be sufficiently
balanced that an enormous variety of strategies are competitive, and the
vast majority of printed cards see some play (though not necessarily with
the same frequency).

The danger of overpowered and broken cards is that they will dominate the
game to the extent that most cards become wallpaper by comparison, and he
who designs a competitive deck will have only, say, the most powerful 10%
of cards printed to choose from. He must, in other words, not be choosing
from 1000 cards, but from the 100 best cards. Thus the viable card set is
reduced by 90%.

It is acceptable that cards have slightly different power levels (say from
2 to 4 on the above scale), provided only that the power levels are not so
different that the 2s never see play in comparison to the 4s.

A card is "broken" when its presence actually reduces player design
options. Once these are gotten rid of, you still will have variable
power levels, but be at a point where banning the new "top cards" actually
reduces variety rather than increasing it. It is at this point that the
banning/fixing should stop.

I hope this rambling message is comprehensible.

valid defense against RtI. One could say that you should put vampiric
disease on all of his minions, have multiple Strained Blood Supply, XTC
lace blood all of his minions, and Cryptic Mission him clean... (heeh.. I
had a deck that did that... was actually viable with a nice SPTR banned
list. I love this game.), and would that be a defense against RtI?

Not really. The problem with RtI is that it can do the work of multiple
cards all by itself, and do it with absolutely no hint that it was going
to do so... A Bruise and Bleed, a Combat deck, a Stealth and bleed... Any
of these can suddenly just kill you and it is over. You can't expect to
have defenses for this card successful on any particular predator,
whether or not they have a hint of playing the card, and have it ready at
all times, just because the card exists.

The only real defenses for this card are all in the "broken" camp:

Direct Intervention
Archon Investigation
Protected Resources

If you don't feel these cards are broken, then stop now. Start a new
thread. Let's debate it. But, given that they are (my starting
premises), that means your only real consistent answers are other broken
cards (or Bounce).

[Re: Feeling that the Problem others have is not the Card but Combos with
the Card]
> a
> point i have made repeatedly, and that has never been answered, is that if
> you ban a card because you don't like a combo in which it is involved,
> then someone will invent a new combo involving different cards that kicks
> ass.

RtI does more than just "kick ass". It literally forces an opponent to
have dedicated cards to it.

OTOH, let's say we have a combo deck (RL example: a friends Ravnos
Trap/Drawing Out The Beast/ Fortitude deck)... In combats, this deck
could regularly torporize nearly any combat deck that it faces... With
Rush, and Bruise n Bleed tactics, it was able to get into combats, and
light intercept, it could block the hunters trying to recover. It would
get into combat with its "KickAss" combo. Some of the newer players
would constantly complain about the deck and its over-effectiveness.
Did it have to be banned, or some part of it banned? No. Standard
combat defenses were fine against the deck. The deck would tend to trump
Weapon or Brujah combat, but lose worse to S:CE and other Fortitude
combat than other combat decks.

You see, the banning of these few singular cards, or the rewriting of
them, wil NOT cause mass bannings because combos themselves aren't the
problem. The problem are cards that SCREAM: Deal With Me. RtI is such a
card.

> Then you will get fed up about that, and you will want to ban another
> card, and so on until we all end up playing Uno. Doesn't this seem a
> somewhat futile exercise to you? Don't you think it might be fun to accept
> that there are clever chaps and chappesses out there who WILL come up with
> spiffy combos, and instead of trying to sabotage their efforts by changing
> the rules, try to beat them at their own game by inventing better combos?

The problem with an imbalanced card set is that it actually LIMITs the
number of viable combos. Since deck space needs to be dedicated to these
cards, the removal of these cards frees up deck space. Some combos
simply cannot compete with the overpowered nature of these broken cards
as well, and their removal clears up space for other combos.

To use an example from another game, Magic:

The existence of Power Cards at the ProTourLA98 (Cursed Scroll) limited
the number of viable decks to roughly 4. Pros and players everywhere
called for the banning of the card previous to the tourney, and testing
from all over the world (there was ambiguity if it would be legal or not,
and thus decks were tested in both environments) showed that the number
of viable decks more than TRIPLED with the banning of one card.
Currently for ProTour Rome Qualifiers, that card is banned, and the
number of viable deck types seems extremely large.

Broken cards limit the number of viable options, not increase them.

Pretend, for a moment that RTI didn't exist. The number of viable deck

power (in terms of swing effect) of RTI is that of SEVERAL bleed cards,
